t: Allocate Mailboxes — Interval DP with Median Cost
o: We must place k mailboxes on a line of n houses so the sum of each house's distance to its nearest mailbox is minimized. The key structural fact: if we sort the houses and decide which contiguous groups of houses share a mailbox, then within one group the optimal mailbox position is the median, and the cost is computable in O(1) with prefix sums. So the problem reduces to partitioning a sorted array into at most k contiguous segments minimizing total segment cost — a classic interval DP. Constraints (n ≤ 100) make an O(n² · k) DP trivially fast. In Example 1, houses [1,4,8,10,20] split into [1,4], [8,10], [20] giving cost 3+2+0=5; in Example 2, [2,3,5] costs 3 (median 3) and [12,18] costs 6 (median 15), total 9.
k: After sorting, an optimal assignment always assigns each mailbox to a contiguous block of houses, so we only need to choose where to cut.
For a fixed group of houses, placing the mailbox at their median minimizes total absolute distance.
Cost of serving houses i..j by one mailbox can be computed in O(1) using prefix sums: cost = (prefix[j+1]-prefix[mid]) - (prefix[mid]-prefix[i]) adjusted for parity of the group size.

a.i: Try every way to cut the sorted array into at most k contiguous groups via recursion: for each start index, try every possible end of the first group, pay its median cost, and recurse on the rest. Memoize on (start, groups left) to avoid exponential blowup. This is the most direct translation of the insight that groups must be contiguous.
s: Sort houses and precompute prefix sums.
Define cost(i,j) = minimal total distance to serve houses i..j with one mailbox (median-based, O(1) via prefix sums).
dp(i, m) = min over j >= i of cost(i,j) + dp(j+1, m-1), with dp = 0 when all remaining groups allowed or no houses left.
a.t: O(n^2 * k) time — n^2 states, each trying up to n transition points; sorting adds O(n log n).
a.sp: O(n^2) for the memo table plus O(n) recursion depth.

a.i: Same recurrence as Approach 1 but computed iteratively: first tabulate cost[i][j] for every pair, then fill dp[j][m] = minimum cost to serve the first j houses with m mailboxes. Bottom-up avoids recursion overhead and makes the structure explicit: dp[j][m] = min over i < j of dp[i][m-1] + cost(i, j-1).
s: Compute cost[i][j] for all 0 <= i <= j < n in O(1) each using the median formula.
Initialize dp[j][1] = cost(0, j-1) for all j.
For m from 2..k and j from m..n: dp[j][m] = min over i in [m-1, j-1] of dp[i][m-1] + cost(i, j-1).
a.t: O(n^2 * k) time — O(n^2) cost table plus n^2*k DP transitions, each O(1); well within limits for n ≤ 100.
a.sp: O(n^2) for the cost table and DP table (can be reduced to O(n·k) by computing cost on the fly).

w: In an interview, lead with the two key observations (contiguity after sorting, median optimality), then present the bottom-up DP as the main solution — it's clean and clearly optimal here. Common pitfalls: forgetting to sort first; using the mean instead of the median for the mailbox position; off-by-one errors in the prefix-sum cost formula (test it on both even- and odd-sized groups); and allowing more mailboxes than houses (k ≤ n guarantees feasibility, so dp[n][k] is always finite). Edge cases: k = n gives answer 0; single house gives 0. Follow-ups: prove why the median minimizes sum of absolute deviations, handle duplicate house positions, or extend to weighted houses or 2D placements (which breaks contiguity and becomes much harder).
